title: The plan
markdown:
# The plan: a UK hair-loss service for men and women

Final blueprint, written 24 November 2026 for the owner, a UK pharmacist independent prescriber. It follows the
judge's decision in `drafts/judging.md`: build the **Clinical Precision** concept (CP) as the base, add the
**Women-first** pathway (WF) as a second front door into the same service, and wrap it in the **Value-and-trust**
fair-deal promises (VT) at CP's price level.

The blueprint is five files:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `plan.md` (this file) | The company on one page, why now, how we beat each rival, the business model, the first year in brief |
| `products.md` | Every product, its price and estimated cost, and the 6 products none of the UK companies studied is seen to offer |
| `engine.md` | The consultation question by question, the rules, the treatment ladder and the follow-up schedule |
| `launch.md` | Phases, team, suppliers, prices and unit economics, marketing within the law, the numbers to watch |
| `risks.md` | The risk register and the compliance checklist before launch |

---

## 0. How sure is this?

- **Built only from this project's files.** No new web research was done for this blueprint. Facts come from the
  five fact-checked files in `foundations/`, the cross-company files in `synthesis/`, the 19 company digests and the
  three drafts. Where a foundations file was corrected in its verification log, the corrected text is used.
- **Evidence marks on rivals.** **\*** = could not be walked live (bot checks): **Voy\***, **Hers (US)\***,
  **Oxford Online Pharmacy\***. **†** = still in final review when this work started (their stage 2 data is
  complete): **Sons†**, **Ro†**. **‡** = never independently verified: **XYON‡**. For **every** company, what
  happens after the sign-in wall is described from public documents or served code, **not watched**. Rivals may do
  more privately than we credit.
- **Unread references.** NICE CKS, the BNF and the UKTIS pregnancy monographs could not be opened by the research. The
  full oral minoxidil consensus paper was confirmed only partly first-hand for men. **No dose in this blueprint is
  final until these are read** (`risks.md`, checklist).
- **Money figures are estimates.** No file holds a wholesale price, a courier rate or any UK rival's cost to win a
  customer. Every price is a proposal until two wholesalers have quoted.
- **[reviewed: corrected] A commercial review (24 November 2026) tested every market figure, rival fact, price and
  money estimate.** Its full log is at the end of `launch.md`. The three changes that matter most: (1) break-even must
  include the cost of replacing patients who leave, and at a £100 cost to win a customer the plan works only if about
  3% or fewer leave each month; (2) the £60 "cost to win a customer" has no benchmark behind it; (3) most of the edge
  can be copied by a rival within weeks, so the lasting edge is the women's pathway and the cost of real clinical care.
- **Not legal or tax advice.** The regulation file recommends legal and regulatory advice before launch.

**Labels used in all five files.** **[proposal]** = our plan, not a fact. **[estimate]** = worked out by us from
figures in the files. **[assumption]** = a planning number with no source; replace it with a quote. **[our view]** = a
judgement. **[to verify]** = must be checked before launch. A source in brackets, such as **[clinical-men 3.1]**,
points to that section of a file in `foundations/` or `synthesis/`; **[CP 4.5]**, **[WF 4.4]**, **[VT 5.8]** and
**[judging 5]** point to the drafts and the judge's file in `blueprint/drafts/`.

**Words used here.** *Pattern hair loss*: the common inherited type (temples and crown in men; a wider parting in
women). *Shedding* (telogen effluvium, TE): sudden, all-over hair fall about 3 months after a trigger, which usually
regrows by itself. *Licensed*: the medicine has a UK licence for that use. *Off-label*: a licensed medicine used
outside its licence (for example minoxidil tablets for hair). *Special*: an unlicensed medicine made for one named
patient. *POM*: prescription-only medicine. *GSL*: general sale list (any shop may sell it). *Tier A*: questions plus
photos, reviewed by a prescriber. *Tier B*: Tier A plus a call, checked blood pressure, blood tests where needed and a
GP letter; every off-label tablet is Tier B. *Contribution*: what is left from a monthly payment after the medicine,
post, card fees, clinician time and similar direct costs.

---

## 1. The company on one page

### 1.1 Name options (pick one, then check it) [proposal]

| Option | Why it fits both sexes | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Parting & Crown** | Names the two places women (parting) and men (crown) usually thin | Check for clashes in hair and beauty |
| **Measured** (for example "Measured Hair Care") | Says the promise: progress is measured with photos, not guessed | A common word: ask a trade mark attorney how to protect it |
| **Kindred Hair** | Pattern loss runs in families; warm, not clinical | Says less about diagnosis |
| **Root Cause** | Says "we find the cause first" in two words | **WF's warning:** an ordinary phrase, so a trade mark may be hard to register or defend |

Before using any name [to verify]: Companies House (including "sensitive words"), the UK trade mark register, the web
address and social handles. **Never** put a prescription medicine in the name or web address (MHRA Blue Guide
Appendix 6 [uk-regulation 2.2]). **No "Doctor" or "Dr"**: the prescribers are pharmacists, and the website must say so
[uk-regulation 3.2].

### 1.2 The promise

> **"We find out why your hair is thinning before we treat it. A named pharmacist stays with you. You see the full
> price before you sign up, and you can leave any time."**

It promises **care, never results**. A results promise is read as a guarantee that a medicine works (ASA ruling
against Numan, March 2024 [uk-regulation key fact 14]). It names no medicine, so it can go on the home page and in
adverts [uk-regulation, "You can"].

### 1.3 Who it serves

**Two front doors, one service.** Men and women arrive through their own landing pages and guides, then use the same
engine, prescribers and terms.

| Group | Why they come to us |
|---|---|
| Men 18+ with gradual thinning at the temples or crown | A real diagnosis, licensed medicines first, a fair monthly price without prepaying, and follow-up of mood and sexual function on finasteride |
| Men worried about finasteride, or who had side effects on it | Balanced counselling, a recorded baseline, and properly dosed routes without finasteride |
| Women 18+ with a widening parting, including in perimenopause and after the menopause | A women's pathway that acts on periods, PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome), menopause, HRT, contraception and pregnancy plans; blood tests when needed; spironolactone that can be stepped up. 6 of the 12 UK companies studied treat men only [cross-company 4.9] |
| Women and men with sudden shedding (after a baby, illness, crash dieting, a weight-loss injection or a new medicine) | We say what it is, check for causes, and do not sell a long-term prescription they do not need. Free |
| Women who are pregnant, trying to conceive or breastfeeding | A free advice route instead of a refusal |
| Women with early traction loss (from tight styles) | Free advice to stop the pulling first; treatment only if a prescriber decides |
| People let down by "tick-box" services | A named prescriber who looks at their photos, and a plan and price they see before paying |

**Not for (we say so on screen, with a next step, before taking any details):** under-18s; anyone with signs of
scarring, bald patches, eyebrow or eyelash loss, a receding hairline (women), rapid male-type hormone signs (women) or
illness symptoms (referred); people with thoughts of self-harm in the last month (crisis help on screen); people on
gender-affirming hormones (a prescriber call until a written protocol exists [to verify]).

**Where:** **England and Scotland at launch** (Scotland once the "English service treating patients in Scotland" check
is cleared [to verify]). **Wales after advice:** the Welsh rules were not checked [uk-regulation 4.3]. **Northern
Ireland: not until advice is taken:** a different pharmacy regulator applies and it was not researched
[uk-regulation, missing item 2].

### 1.4 The edge in seven lines

1. **We diagnose; they sell.** Photos from every new patient, the trigger question as a timing question, weight-loss
   injections asked by name, and blood tests when the story points to them. No UK company in the set does all of this
   [cross-company 4.6, 5].
2. **Real stops, first.** Nobody gives contact details to be told "no". Every stop gives a reason and a next step.
3. **Licensed first, written ladder.** Nobody publishes a stepped, licensed-first plan [cross-company 5].
4. **Separate medicines at evidence doses.** No "extra strength", no fixed combination pills, no vitamin passengers.
5. **Women's medicine done properly.** Stepped spironolactone, and women's minoxidil tablets from a licensed tablet,
   which none of the 12 UK companies studied is seen to sell [products-prices 5.2]. **[reviewed: corrected]** Not
   "no UK rival": Oxford Online Pharmacy\* stocks licensed 2.5 mg minoxidil tablets and runs a women's programme with
   blood tests whose medicine is not named, so it may already do this privately; a few small private dermatology
   services prescribe spironolactone tablets [products-prices 3.5, 4.1, 4.3; uk-sweep 4d, not fact-checked].
6. **A named prescriber for follow-up and side effects**, kept apart from sales.
7. **The Fair Deal:** pay only if approved, one price a month, a reminder before every charge, two-tap cancel, refunds
   tied to our care, never to results. Built for the January 2027 subscription rules. **[reviewed: corrected]** Those
   rules will require reminders, easy exit and cooling-off in **every** rival's new contracts from 1 January 2027 (if
   made as drafted) [uk-regulation key fact 24]. Boots and Voy\* (older terms) already take payment only after
   approval, and Hims UK refunds in full if the clinician does not approve [digests]. What stays ours alone is no
   prepaying, no first-order discounts and refunds tied to care.

**[reviewed: corrected] How fast could a rival copy this?** Lines 1 to 4 and 6 are mostly questions, screens, wording
and staffing. A funded rival could copy the visible parts within weeks; LloydsPharmacy already stops on screen and
shows prices before sign-in, and Sons† owns UK licences for both men's licensed medicines. What is slow and costly to
copy is the clinical work behind them: about £3.90 to £4.50 of prescriber time per patient a month in year 1, against about £1.50 in
the market file's typical brand [market-economics 5.6; `launch.md` 5.1], plus a women's pathway with bloods,
contraception checks and stepped doses. Treat the edge as a head start of months, not a moat. Competitor by
competitor: `launch.md`, Commercial review log, part E.

### 1.5 The model in five lines

- A pharmacist-only prescribing service, dispensed from a GPhC-registered pharmacy (our own, or shared premises at
  first). No doctor or nurse in treatment, so no CQC registration in England [uk-regulation key fact 20].
- Monthly plans at one all-in price per calendar month: prescriber, every review, photo checks, messages and tracked
  delivery. Blood tests extra at a published price. Shedding, pregnancy and traction advice free.
- Mid-market prices: finasteride £18 to £20, two medicines £32 to £38 a month [proposal].
- About **£7.55 contribution per patient a month in year 1 and £10.50 in year 2** [estimate, `launch.md` 5].
  **[reviewed: corrected]** The blueprint said £8.14 and £10.98; the review costs the second pharmacist's check at the
  plan's own rate.
- Break-even before marketing at about **1,480 active patients** on a lean set-up and **2,650 to 2,890** on a standard
  one [estimate]. **[reviewed: corrected]** That figure ignores the cost of winning new patients to replace those who
  leave. Including it, at a £100 cost to win a customer, the lean set-up needs about **1,900** active patients if 3%
  leave each month, about **3,800** if 5% leave, and cannot realistically break even if 7% or more leave
  (`launch.md` 5.5). These leaving rates are scenarios: no UK rival publishes one.

---

## 2. Why now

| What is happening | The fact | Source |
|---|---|---|
| A large group, mostly untreated | Roughly 12 million UK men and 3.4 to 6.2 million UK women have pattern hair loss **[estimate in the source]**. In 2005 fewer than 10% of affected European men were on treatment | [market-economics key facts 4, 5] |
| Online is the fastest-growing channel; women the faster-growing sex | Online pharmacies +12.7% a year; women +9.1% a year (one research firm's unaudited forecast; use for direction only). **[reviewed: corrected]** Both are **global** forecasts, not UK ones | [market-economics key fact 9] |
| The giants are consolidating, and they lead with men | Hims & Hers (US$2.35bn revenue in 2025) now owns Hims UK, ZAVA (the platform behind Superdrug's online doctor) and Juniper UK. Voy (£227m in 2025) and Numan (£69m in 2024) grew mainly on weight loss. **[reviewed: corrected]** ZAVA's accounts say its growth came from weight loss; for Voy and Numan this is an inference, because their accounts do not split sales by condition | [market-economics 3.1, key facts 10, 13, 15, 16] |
| Women are badly served | 6 of 12 UK companies treat men only. The only anti-androgen for women is a fixed 44 mg compounded capsule (Hers UK). No UK women's pathway acts on periods, PCOS, menopause, HRT or contraception. **[reviewed: corrected]** True of the 12 companies studied, before sign-in. Outside them, a few small private dermatology services prescribe spironolactone tablets, City Skin Clinic sells topical spironolactone, and Dermatica (a large skincare subscription) began treating women's thinning with photos and a dermatology team in February 2026 (market sweep, not fact-checked) | [cross-company 4.9; products-prices 4.3; uk-sweep 4d] |
| Weight-loss injections cause shedding, and nobody asks | Hair loss is a listed side effect: 2.5% on semaglutide 2.4 mg and 4.9% on tirzepatide against 1.0% on placebo; most recover while continuing | [clinical-women key fact 25; cross-company 4.6] |
| Regulators are acting on the shortcuts rivals rely on | GPhC statutory enforcement against Voy's pharmacy (August 2026), partly for prescription-medicine advertising; MHRA strengthened finasteride warnings on 11 May 2026; repeated ASA rulings against Hims, Numan and Manual/Voy. **[reviewed: corrected]** Voy's pharmacy **met all standards again on 13 October 2026** after it "strengthened its governance, introduced more clinical checking" and tightened oversight of its promotion. Rivals can and do fix these gaps quickly | [uk-regulation 3.5, key facts 12 to 15, 21] |
| Subscription law is changing | DMCCA subscription rules (reminders, easy exit, cooling-off) expected for new contracts from 1 January 2027 (still a draft on 23 November 2026). **[reviewed: corrected]** They bind every rival's new contracts too, so easy exit stops being a point of difference | [uk-regulation key fact 24] |
| Customers are angry about the same things | Cancelling or renewals in 35% of negative reviews; main complaint in a hand-read sample: delivery or stock about 28%, "no results" about 22%, subscription or refund about 18%; refunds refused mentioned in 24%. **[reviewed: corrected]** These come from keyword screens of Trustpilot samples, and more than half of the roughly 1,860 screened negative reviews are about US companies (Hims US, Hers US, Keeps, Happy Head, Nutrafol and others); the 28/22/18 split rests on 68 hand-read reviews | [customer-voice summary, 1.2, 1.3; cross-company 4.10] |
| Prices are being driven down by first-order discounts | First orders at about half price (Voy 50% off; Hair + Me £14.99 then £34.99); Dr Fox sets a floor of £10 for 28 finasteride tablets | [market-economics key facts 21, 22] |
| Retention is the unknown that decides the business | No UK rival publishes its cost to win a customer or churn. Hims lost about 103,000 subscribers in a quarter in which it trimmed marketing (the cause is an inference) | [market-economics key fact 11; 10] |

**What this means [our view]:** a service built to the higher standard now loses nothing when the next ruling lands,
and can say lawfully what rivals cannot: service facts (a diagnosis, a named pharmacist, honest terms).

**[reviewed: corrected] Is the market big enough?** No trustworthy figure exists for UK online hair-loss prescribing;
the market file's own low-confidence judgement is "tens of millions of pounds a year, not hundreds"
[market-economics 2.2]. Break-even in the review's scenarios needs about £0.6m (lean) to £1.2m (standard) of revenue a
year, which is a small share of that. So the market is not the limit; the cost of winning and keeping patients is.

---

## 3. How we beat each named competitor

Rival prices are as found on 23 to 24 November 2026 [products-prices 3]. Our prices are proposals. **We never name a
rival in an advert**; this table is for the owner only.

### 3.1 UK companies

| Rival | Where they are strong | Where they fall short | How we beat them |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hims UK** (with **Hers UK** for women) | Money (group marketing US$919m in 2025); a friction-free quiz; "Delete my answers" and 7-day storage; £16.50 a month on a 6-month prepaid plan | All 42 quiz answers change nothing; nothing shown before the email; compounded products in one fixed strength; cancel by message to support only. Hers UK asks her name on screen one; spironolactone fixed at 44 mg (below the 50 mg NHS start) with no step-up [obs, code] | Answers act on screen; result and price before an account; licensed, separate medicines; stepped spironolactone from licensed tablets; monthly without prepaying; two-tap cancel. We copy the data controls |
| **Voy\*** (formerly Manual) | Size; in-house pharmacy; delivery in under 48 hours; pause, switch, cancel in the account [docs] | Pop-up takes an email, then says "not eligible"; headline prices are first-order offers on 6-month plans; 10% minoxidil; oral minoxidil as unlicensed capsules; GPhC found it did not independently verify answers (March 2026) and took enforcement action (August 2026) [obs pop-up; docs]. **[reviewed: corrected]** Re-inspected 13 October 2026: standards met, with "more clinical checking" [uk-regulation 3.5] | Stops before details; licensed tablets; 5% at most; independent checks (photos, ID, GP, two blood pressure readings, calls); one standing price. Match its account controls and delivery speed. *Its quiz was never seen.* **[reviewed: corrected]** Voy has fixed its checking gap on paper, sells weight-loss injections (so it already holds the patients most likely to shed) and has a women's dermatologist lead: it is the rival best placed to copy us fastest |
| **Hair + Me** | Very easy (40% of its praise); pet question; pregnancy route; two 0 to 10 wellbeing scores [obs] | No medical answer changes anything (68 replays); bag says only "Personalised treatment"; all 16 formulas compounded; photos optional and after payment; bills every 4 weeks (£34.99 = £37.91 a calendar month) [obs, verified] | Named plan before payment; licensed first; photos before the first prescription; calendar-month billing. We copy the pet question and the outcome scores |
| **Sons†** | Its own UK licences for finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil 5% spray; PHQ-2 mood questions; NHS record consent [code, docs] | Men only; no plan or price until name, email, phone, date of birth and password; no crisis help for "nearly every day"; silent removals; "I don't mind" = unlicensed capsule; cancel by email; retention offers of 40% then 50% off [obs, code] | Women too; crisis screen; result first; licensed default; same-route cancel; no retention discounts. We copy the mood screen and record consent. Its 5% spray could be one of our stock lines |
| **Numan** | Shows the full offer and every price before sign-in; the only early-shedding warning seen before sign-in; written clinician instructions [obs, verified] | No crisis help for suicidal thoughts in the past year; product links bypass its filter; opt-outs ignored; "Review your answers" undoes stops; any blood-pressure answer removes topical minoxidil; men only [obs, verified] | Crisis question never skipped; one rule set on every route; opt-outs honoured; stops final; three outcomes, not two; women |
| **Dr Fox** | **Price:** finasteride £7.25 a month on 168 tablets; full total before sign-in; no subscription; a doctor approves every order [obs] | No diagnosis at all; "change your answer and continue"; Regaine sold with high blood pressure; no step-up, follow-up or women [obs, verified] | Diagnosis, follow-up, a ladder, women. **We do not beat it on price** and say so |
| **Treated** | Full price list before contact details; fast questionnaire; clear dutasteride acknowledgements [obs] | Men only; answers barely change the offer; any mental illness ends the consultation (minoxidil too); no photos; age asked only at checkout [obs, verified] | Diagnosis and photos; mood handled by the MHRA's "ask and decide", never a block on minoxidil; women |
| **Philip Kingsley** | Trichology brand; a real paid consultation route; scalp-first approach; women's quiz [obs, code] | Full registration before any result; a leading space breaks its blood-pressure rule; compounded products only; prescriber not named publicly [code checked live] | Result before details; tested rules; licensed first; named pharmacist prescriber |
| **Boots Online Doctor** | Trusted brand; store collection; pay only if approved; server labels risky orders [obs, code] | Nine red flags at once reached the same ID and payment screen; men only; one-off orders [obs, verified] | Stops on screen before data; a plan with follow-up; women |
| **Superdrug Online Doctor** (platform now owned by Hims & Hers) | The only UK company seen to ask for photos before ordering (unusual men's patterns) [obs] | Men's list never changes; no men's mood question; women get Regaine and supplements only, still offered in pregnancy [obs, verified] | Photos from everyone; mood screen; pregnancy handled properly; a real women's range |
| **LloydsPharmacy Online Doctor** | **Best engine in the UK set:** acts on most risks before sign-in, shows prices, real treatment history, pets, crisis help, licensed oral minoxidil [obs, verified] | Silent, blunt removals (any blood-pressure answer removes the spray); recommended out-of-stock packs; men only [obs] | One-line reasons; prescriber-decides outcome; never recommend what cannot ship; women. We copy its history and smart skipping |
| **Oxford Online Pharmacy\*** | Value: finasteride £9.17 a month on 168 tablets; licensed oral minoxidil; the only women's programme with blood tests (£75.99) [docs] | Payment before the prescriber decides; the women's medicine is not named and other pages refuse oral treatment for women; new consultation for every reorder [docs] | A named, explained women's plan; pay only if approved; follow-up. *Desk research only; treat as unconfirmed* |

**[reviewed: corrected] Rivals for the women's front door that the table leaves out** (UK market sweep, not
fact-checked): **Dermatica**, a large prescription-skincare subscription (8,760 Trustpilot reviews), started treating
women's thinning in February 2026 with photos and a dermatology team; its hair page returned "not found" on
23 November 2026, so check it is still open. **City Skin Clinic** sells bespoke serums with topical spironolactone
(£120 per 3 months). **SkinDoc and Midland Skin** (private dermatology) are reported to prescribe spironolactone
tablets after a video or online consultation [uk-sweep 1, 4d]. Our women's edge is the depth of the pathway, not
being the only one.

### 3.2 US companies (for ideas, not direct rivals)

| Rival | What we take | What we avoid |
|---|---|---|
| **Hims (US)** | Wide choice of forms for the same drug; "Why we ask" notes | A quiz where no answer changes the outcome; 10-month prepaid plans [obs, verified] |
| **Hers (US)\*** | Finasteride only after the menopause (we go further: never for women) | 30% of its negative reviews mention unwarned early shedding [customer-voice 3.7]; result behind an account [docs] |
| **Keeps** | An honest "medicine is unlikely to help" screen for very advanced loss | "You're approved" before any medical question; compounded dutasteride as the default [obs] |
| **Ro†** | Explained stop screens for women; scalp photos and outcome scores for women | The same compounded spray for every man; no stops for men [obs, code] |
| **Happy Head** | Date-of-birth re-entry that must match | Product chosen before safety questions; red flags do nothing [obs] |
| **Strut** | A crisis screen that cannot be clicked past | No safety screening; dose chosen before medical questions [obs] |
| **XYON‡** | A pregnancy stop before any data is taken | Dutasteride gel "for both" sexes. *Never verified* |

### 3.3 Where we do not win on price, and say so

- **Dr Fox** (finasteride £7.25 to £14.90 a month) and **Oxford\*** (£9.17 to £13.99) stay cheaper for a tablet
  alone. We win on everything around the tablet [products-prices 3.2].
- **Hims UK's** compounded chew is £16.50 a month, but only on a 6-month plan paid up front (£99) [products-prices 3.5].
- **Sons'†** own licensed 5% spray is £15 a month on a 12-month plan; our scalp minoxidil is £22 a month,
  paid monthly, with a prescriber and photo reviews [products-prices 3.3]. **[reviewed: corrected]** Whether the
  12-month plan is paid up front was not recorded. Dr Fox also sells the same Sons 5% spray at £19.95 for one month
  and £14.98 a month on 6 months, with no subscription, so a man who wants only the spray can pay less elsewhere.
- **Numan's** finasteride on annual billing (£20 a month) matches our top finasteride price.

**At our chosen prices [estimate]:** a year of finasteride costs £216 to £240, against £240 at Numan (annual
billing), £245 at Boots, £272 at Sons† and £276 at Hims UK [products-prices 3.2]. **[reviewed: corrected]** The
same source puts a year at Dr Fox at about £100 to £116 with fees and delivery; leaving it out made the comparison
look better than it is. A two-medicine plan at £32 a month
sits at the UK median for a **6-month prepaid** plan (£31.50) and well below the **single-month** median (£43.50)
[products-prices 3.6], without prepaying.

**[reviewed: corrected] Women's prices against the market.** Our scalp minoxidil for women is £26 a month. Rivals:
Voy\* £24 a month on its main page (£14.99 on advert pages), Hers UK from £13 (from £20 with spironolactone), Hair + Me
£37.91 a calendar month, Philip Kingsley 3% drops £36 [products-prices 4.1]. Regaine for Women is sold without a
consultation for about £25 a pack at Superdrug and £27.77 (2%) or £34.80 (5% foam) at Oxford\*; how long a pack lasts
is still [to verify]. So in phase 2 (Tier A only) a woman pays us about a shop price, or more, for a general-sale
product; she is buying the diagnosis and follow-up, and blood tests cost extra. Say so plainly, and measure whether
women convert at £26.

---

## 4. The business model

### 4.1 How it works

| Part | Our choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Who prescribes | Pharmacist independent prescribers only, named on the website with GPhC number | No CQC registration in England [uk-regulation key fact 20]; the GPhC requires the prescriber's name, number and profession online [key fact 17] |
| Who dispenses | A GPhC-registered pharmacy; a **second pharmacist** checks every prescription; patients told they may use another pharmacy | GPhC prescriber guidance [uk-regulation key fact 19] |
| What people pay | One all-in price per calendar month, whatever the delivery rhythm; no first-order, retention or plan-length discounts | Customers value one honest price; the GPhC treated a first-month discount as an improper incentive at Voy [uk-regulation 3.5]. **[reviewed: corrected]** That discount was on a weight-loss medicine, not a hair product [uk-regulation verification row 29]; the principle still applies to any prescription medicine. Commercial cost: rivals' first orders are 40% to 57% off, so our first month will look dearer; the pilot must measure the effect on sign-ups |
| When they pay | Card saved, charged only if a prescriber approves; full refund before dispensing | "Refunds refused" in 24% of negative reviews [cross-company 4.1] |
| What is free | The hair check and result; the shedding programme; the pregnancy and new-mum route; traction advice; free tools (photo tracker, shedding timeline, GP summary) | Trust, first contact and honest triage; selling long-term treatment to shedding feeds "no results" complaints |
| What is extra | Blood tests, at the laboratory's price plus a published handling fee; iron and ketoconazole shampoo at a small published margin | Ordered only when the answer changes the decision |

### 4.2 Price list in one view [proposal; provisional until two wholesalers quote]

| Plan | Price a month |
|---|---|
| Men: finasteride 1 mg | **£18 to £20** (test in the pilot) |
| Men: minoxidil 5% on the scalp, liquid or foam (same price) | **£22** |
| Men: finasteride + scalp minoxidil | **£32** |
| Men: minoxidil tablets (Tier B) / with finasteride | **£22 / £36** |
| Men: dutasteride (step 3, Tier B) / with scalp minoxidil / with minoxidil tablets | **£22 / £34 / £38** |
| Women: minoxidil on the scalp, 5% foam or 2% solution (same price) | **£26** |
| Women: minoxidil tablets (Tier B) | **£20** |
| Women: spironolactone (Tier B) / with minoxidil tablets / with scalp minoxidil | **£18 / £32 / £38** |
| Shedding programme, pregnancy route, traction advice | **Free** |

Why scalp minoxidil is one price per sex: customers choose a base by feel, not by price (VT's product-feel rule). The
single price sits between CP's £17 liquid and £24 foam so that branded foam, costed cautiously at 50% of price, does
not lose money (`products.md` 1; `launch.md` 5).

### 4.3 The money in brief [estimate; inputs in `launch.md` 5]

## 6. Summary in ten lines

1. **What:** a UK online hair-loss service for men and women, led by a pharmacist independent prescriber, with two
   front doors (men's and women's) into one engine.
2. **Promise:** we find out why before we treat; a named pharmacist stays with you; full price first; leave any time.
3. **Edge:** diagnosis first (photos, trigger timing, weight-loss injections, targeted bloods), real stops before
   contact details, licensed first with a written ladder, separate medicines at evidence doses.
4. **Women:** stepped spironolactone (online ceiling 100 mg) and minoxidil tablets from a licensed tablet (ceiling
   2.5 mg), which none of the 12 UK companies studied is seen to sell (Oxford\* may do it privately; see 1.4); free
   pregnancy, shedding and traction routes.
5. **Fair Deal:** pay only if approved, one price a month, reminders, two-tap cancel, refunds tied to care, never
   results.
6. **Prices [proposal]:** finasteride £18 to £20; scalp minoxidil £22 (men) or £26 (women); two medicines £32 to £38.
7. **Money [estimate]:** about £7.55 a patient a month in year 1 and £10.50 in year 2; payback about 15 months at a
   £100 cost to win a customer, if the patient stays; break-even about 1,480 patients lean before replacing leavers,
   about 1,900 once leavers are replaced (if only 3% leave a month), and out of reach if 7% or more leave.
   **[reviewed: corrected]** (blueprint: £8 and £11; break-even 1,400 lean, 2,500 to 2,700 standard, ignoring leavers).
8. **Law:** advertise the condition and the service only; no medicine names in adverts; GSL product adverts kept
   apart from the consultation, or dropped, on legal advice. **[reviewed: corrected]** Also get adviser sign-off for
   the home-page "from £18" line (only prescription plans reach £18), keep reviews that name medicines off marketing
   pages, and check the data basis for marketing emails to patients.
9. **Launch:** a 100-patient closed pilot, then Tier A, then capped Tier B; England and Scotland first.
10. **Biggest risks:** thin early margins against rich rivals, a clinical or advertising slip, and breaking our own
    promises at scale; each has a control in `risks.md`. **[reviewed: corrected]** The biggest commercial risk is
    retention: if more than about 6% to 7% of patients leave each month, no realistic size breaks even at £100 to
    win a customer.
